title: Let's: suggestions and wishes
intro: This unit adds two moods for what the speaker wants to happen. The optative says **let me** and **let's**: *Kapıyı açayım mı?* (Shall I open the door?), *Gidelim mi?* (Shall we go?). The third-person imperative says **let him** and **let them**: *Ali gelsin* (Let Ali come). On these forms rest the wishes Turks say every day, from *Kolay gelsin* to *Geçmiş olsun*, and the little word that gets things moving: *hadi*.

sections.title: Gidelim mi? Let's, let me, shall I

blocks.text: The optative (*istek kipi*) is the speaker's own wish or suggestion. In today's Turkish you use it in the first person: `-(y)AyIm` for **let me**, **shall I**, and `-(y)AlIm` for **let's**, **shall we**.

The A is e or a by two-way harmony, the I follows four-way harmony: *geleyim, gelelim; yapayım, yapalım; göreyim, görelim; duralım*. After a stem that ends in a vowel, a buffer y comes first: *okuyayım, okuyalım; bekleyeyim, bekleyelim; başlayalım*.

rows.en: let me come, shall I come

blocks.text: **Negative.** `-mA` comes first, then a buffer y: *gelmeyeyim* (let me not come), *gelmeyelim* (let's not come), *yapmayalım*.

**Questions.** Put `mI` after the verb. Unlike the tenses with type I endings, nothing moves: the person is already part of the form. *Geleyim mi?* (Shall I come?), *Gidelim mi?* (Shall we go?). With a question word, there is no `mI`: *Ne yapalım?* (What shall we do?)
**Stems** change as they do before the future `-(y)AcAk` ([unit 3](gp-future-stem-changes)): *git-* and *et-* soften to *gid-* and *ed-*, and *de-* and *ye-* become *diy-* and *yiy-*.

rows.en: let me go, shall I go

blocks.text: **Uses.** *Gidelim* suggests; *Gidelim mi?* suggests more gently, as a question. *Kapıyı açayım mı?* offers to do something, and *Ne yapayım?* asks for advice. On its own, the **let me** form announces what you are about to do: *Bir bakayım* (Let me have a look), and in a café *Ben bir çay alayım* (I'll have a tea).

items.en: Shall we go to the cinema this evening?
Shall I open the door?
Let me help you.
What shall we do at the weekend?
It's raining; let's not go out.
I'll have a tea too.

blocks.text: **The other persons.** The optative also has forms for **you**, **he** and **they**: *gelesin, gele, gelesiniz, geleler*. They survive in old texts, folk songs and a few fixed sayings, but everyday Turkish uses the imperative instead: *gel* and *gelin* for **you** ([A1 unit 12](gp-imperative)), and *gelsin* and *gelsinler* for **he** and **they**, in the next section.
*Gidelim* (let's go) is not *gideriz* (we go, we'll go: the aorist of [unit 4](gp-aorist-forms)) or *gideceğiz* (we're going to go). Only the optative suggests.
Compare two offers. *Çay içer misiniz?* ([unit 4](gp-aorist-uses)) asks what the guest would like; *Çay getireyim mi?* (Shall I bring some tea?) offers to act. Both are polite, and hosts use both.

sections.title: Ali gelsin: let him, let them

blocks.text: The imperative of [A1 unit 12](gp-imperative) speaks to **you**. Turkish also has an imperative for **he, she, it** and **they**: the stem + `-sIn`, and `-sInlAr` for **they**. *Ali gelsin* means **let Ali come**, **Ali should come** or **tell Ali to come**: the speaker wants it, and someone else is to do it.

The suffix starts with a consonant, so stems never change: *gitsin, etsin, desin, yesin*. Its vowel follows four-way harmony: *gelsin, yapsın, okusun, görsün*. With a plural subject, *-lAr* can be left out: *Çocuklar yatsın* or *Çocuklar yatsınlar*.
**Questions** ask for a decision about someone else: *Ayşe de gelsin mi?* (Should Ayşe come too? Shall I tell her to come?). The answer often repeats the verb: *Gelsin* (Sure, let her come).

items.en: The children should go to bed early.
Should Ayşe come too?
Mehmet can do the dishes.
The guests can sit in the living room.
Nobody should be late.

blocks.text: Two everyday words are forms of *olmak*: *Olsun* (never mind, so be it, it doesn't matter) and its negative in *Neden olmasın?* (Why not?, literally **why shouldn't it be?**).
`-sIn` after a bare stem is the imperative: *gelsin*, let him come. After a tense or a noun it is the ending for **you**: *gelirsin* (you come), *yorgunsun* (you're tired).
Instructions for a group often use it: *Herkes kemerini taksın* (Everyone should fasten their seat belt). And a host making plans: *Sofrayı çocuklar kursun* (The children can set the table).

sections.title: Kolay gelsin: a wish for every moment

blocks.text: Many everyday formulas are third-person imperatives of *olmak* or *gelmek*: wishes that something may be so. Each belongs to a moment, and leaving it out where Turks expect it can sound cold. Learn each one with its moment and its answer.

head: Wish
Literally
When
Answer
rows: to anyone at work: a shopkeeper, a builder, a colleague at a desk
to someone who is ill, has had an accident or bad luck
to someone eating or about to eat; the cook's answer to thanks
to the cook after a meal, or to anyone who made something for you
for something new: a job, a home, a car, a baby
for something someone has just bought
to someone setting off on a trip
to someone who has lost a relative

blocks.text: Most of these are the `-sIn` of the last section: *ol-sun*, *gel-sin*. *Elinize sağlık* has no verb at all: *sağlık* (health) goes to your hands, *elinize*, in the dative. *Güle güle* is the goodbye of [A1 unit 1](a1-u01): it comes from *gülmek*, to laugh, and means **with a smile**.
The forms with `-InIz` and `-In` are for people you call *siz*. To a friend, say *Eline sağlık*, *Güle güle kullan*, *Güle güle otur*. The wishes in *olsun* don't change.

items.en: Hope the work's going well, Murat Bey!
Sorry to hear that. How are you now?
The meal was delicious, thank you.

items.tr: Yeni bir iş buldum. — Hayırlı olsun!
items.seg: Yeni bir iş buldum. — Hayırlı ol|sun!
items.en: I've found a new job. — Congratulations!
Have a good trip, send us a message!

blocks.text: *Kolay gelsin* is said to strangers too: a waiter, a cashier, workers in the street, the person who comes to fix your heating. It costs nothing and opens every door.
*Geçmiş olsun* is only for bad news, once it has happened. Before an exam or an interview, wish someone *Başarılar* (good luck, literally **successes**) or *Kolay gelsin*.

*Hadi*, or *haydi* in the dictionary and in careful speech, pushes someone to act: **come on**, **let's go**, **go on**. It goes with the optative, the imperative and the third-person imperative, and takes no endings of its own.

head: Turkish
English
rows: All right, he can come too.
Come on then! Off we go!
Come off it! You don't say!

blocks.text: Besides urging, *hadi* can accept something a little reluctantly (*Hadi, o da gelsin*: oh, all right, let him come too) and, in *Hadi canım!*, say that you don't believe what you've just heard. *Bakalım*, in *Hadi bakalım*, is itself an optative: **let's see**, from *bakmak*.

items.en: Come on, hurry up, the film's starting!

items.tr: Hava çok güzel, hadi sahile inelim.
items.seg: Hava çok güzel, hadi sahile in|e|lim.
items.en: The weather is lovely; come on, let's go down to the seaside.
Come on then, everybody get in the car.
Come on, let's have one more tea.

blocks.text: *Hadi* is friendly but direct. With strangers or older people, a polite question is softer: *Gelir misiniz?* ([unit 4](gp-aorist-uses)). And to a group you change the verb, not *hadi*: *Hadi gelin!*
A plan agreed over the phone often ends with *Anlaştık* (Deal, agreed) and *Hadi görüşürüz* (Right, see you).

summary: **Let me**: stem + `-(y)AyIm` (*geleyim, okuyayım*); **let's**: stem + `-(y)AlIm` (*gelelim, okuyalım*). Negative *gelmeyelim*; question *Gelelim mi?*, with nothing moving onto `mI`.
Stems change as before the future: *gidelim, edeyim, diyelim, yiyelim*.
Offers and suggestions: *Kapıyı açayım mı?*, *Gidelim mi?*, *Ne yapalım?*
**Let him, let them**: stem + `-sIn`, `-sInlAr` (*gelsin, gelsinler*); negative *gelmesin*; question *Gelsin mi?* The stem never changes.
*Olsun* (never mind) and *Neden olmasın?* (Why not?) are forms of *olmak*.
Set wishes: *Kolay gelsin* (at work), *Geçmiş olsun* (illness, bad luck), *Afiyet olsun* (eating), *Elinize sağlık* (to the cook), *Hayırlı olsun* (something new), *İyi yolculuklar* (a trip).
*Hadi* or *haydi*: **come on**, with the optative and the imperatives: *Hadi gidelim!*
